How you see the table
Player’s eye: the 3D table from the television camera, so you see every ball. Tap a ball or Get down to go down on the cue for your shot; you’re back on the whole table the moment you play it. The 2D / 3D switch on the table changes it any time, and the game remembers what you chose.
Aiming guide
Short line: the first few inches of the object ball's path, like the line you picture before you get down. You judge the rest. With a guide on, the computer raises its game to match: a little with the short line, more with full paths.

How you see the table
Player’s eye opens the 3D table for every shot in a frame or in practice, from the television camera, and keeps it open while the balls run. The 2D / 3D switch on the table sets this too.
Setting the pace
Swipe: when you press Play, pull the cue back against a spring. The further you pull, the harder you hit; let go to play. Aim and spin are set as usual.
Claude coach (optional) Add your Anthropic API key to get a coach’s write-up of your stats in My game. It’s stored only on this phone. Everything else works without it.

Player’s view

Tap a ball to aim at it and get down on the shot. Tap the cloth to look from that side of the table.

Touch the cloth to aim roughly, then keep your finger down and slide it sideways to turn the line slowly (about 1° for every finger-width). Lift and touch again for a big change. Drag a ball to move it, or onto the rail to take it off. Pinch with two fingers to zoom in on the table; slide two fingers together to scroll the page.

Shot suggestions

Suggest shots gives you the coach’s call: the pot when it’s on, a safety when the pot’s a poor bet, and a snooker when you need one. Safety shots and Snookers show only those. Chances are for a good club player.

    Coaching

    The ideas coaches teach first. Open a lesson, try it on the table with the paths showing, then practise it with the matching round.

    Practice routines

    Standard coaching routines, set up exactly as you would on a real table and scored for you. Levels follow the Cuestars Practice Challenge (Bronze, Silver, Gold) used in UK junior coaching. Shot suggestions work in every routine.

    Coaching courses

    Fifteen courses in order. The skill courses teach one thing at a time; the game courses put them together in real situations, point you back to the skill that let you down, and finish with a mixed test. Each course opens when you finish the one before.

    Trick shots

    Fifteen trick shots, from easiest to the grand finale. Three tries at each, with no guide lines. Stuck? Watch the computer play it, or tap “How do I play it?” for the idea, then the strike and pace, then exactly how.

    Cue ball strike

    Side effects
    Level

    To swerve, raise the butt and add side: the cue ball curls towards the side you use. Strike it high and it bends early; strike it low and it runs straight before bending late. With the cue raised past 20° you can strike further out than the red ring on the cue ball, up to the orange ring, for a bigger massé, but it costs accuracy and can miscue.

      How the physics works

      The table is a full-size 12 ft snooker table (3569 × 1778 mm playing area) with 52.5 mm balls. The cue ball slides on the cloth until friction turns its spin into natural roll, so screw and stun wear off with distance, just as they do on a real table. Collisions between balls pass on the push along the line of centres, which is why a stunned cue ball leaves at right angles to the object ball, top bends it forward and screw bends it back.

      Side changes where the object ball goes in three ways, and you can switch each one off to see what it does. Squirt: the cue ball pushes off line away from the side you use, so right-hand side sends it left of where you aimed. Swerve: because the cue is slightly raised over the rail, the cue ball curls back towards the side used as it slides. Throw: at contact the spinning cue ball drags the object ball sideways, so right-hand side throws it left. Throw is strongest on slow shots. The faint dashed circle is where you aimed; the solid circle is where the cue ball actually made contact.

      With rules on, each shot is refereed: you must hit the ball on first and pot only the ball on. After a red you can play any colour (the first colour you hit counts as the one you nominated), and once the reds have gone the colours go in order. A foul gives your opponent the higher of 4 points or the value of the balls involved, and then you carry on playing. Potted colours go back on their own spots. If a colour’s spot is covered, it goes on the highest-value spot that’s free, and if every spot is covered, as close to its own spot as it can on the line towards the top cushion. Free balls, foul and a miss (with the three-miss rule and the snookers-needed exception), playing again, touching ball, the respotted black and the stalemate re-rack are all included.

      Shot suggestions try each makeable pot with a range of strikes and paces, aiming each one properly to allow for throw and side. They keep the ones that pot fairly and score them by how good the next pot would be from where the cue ball stops, in expected points. So a likely black beats a likely pink, but an easy pink beats a hard black. Shots that still leave good position when struck a little softer or harder are preferred. The pot chances assume a good club player and are a guide for comparing shots, not exact odds.

      Setting up from a photo: the four pockets you tap tell the page exactly how the photo maps onto the table, and from that it works out where the camera was, so it can allow for each ball sitting above the cloth. It then finds everything on the cloth that is ball-sized and not cloth-coloured, and reads each ball’s colour from its lit side. If a pocket is out of shot, press Can’t see this pocket and tap two points along that pocket’s long cushion instead; the page works out where the hidden pocket must be. With carefully placed markers, balls usually land within a centimetre or two of where they really are. Photos taken from higher up and more square-on are more accurate. The photo is processed on your device and is never uploaded.

      The amounts are typical for a snooker cue with a standard tip. Your own cue, tip and cue elevation will change them a little. The pockets are cut to match-table size: corner pockets about 86 mm across (3 3/8 in, the WPBSA template) and middles about 103 mm, with jaws a ball can rattle in. Cushion behaviour is simplified.
